opus-5.5.text:
I think there's been real progress, though it's uneven, and it depends a lot on where you look.

Ten years ago, in many technical fields, being a woman in the room was still quite unusual, and people noticed. Today, at least in AI and computer science, I see more women in PhD programs, leading open-source projects, founding companies, and speaking at major conferences. There's also more awareness. People talk openly about bias in hiring, in promotions, and in who gets credit, and many organizations have put mentorship programs and more transparent evaluation processes in place. That matters, because a lot of the barriers were never explicit rules. They were small, accumulated things: who gets invited to the meeting, who gets the benefit of the doubt, who's assumed to be the "real" engineer.

But I don't want to overstate it. The numbers at the senior levels, like tenured faculty, technical leads, founders who raise large rounds, and investors, still drop off a lot. The pipeline has improved faster than the top of the ladder. And in parts of the world, and in some industries, progress has stalled or even reversed. So I'd say the past decade improved visibility and awareness, and opened more doors at the entry level. The next step is harder: making sure women stay, grow, and get the same access to resources and leadership opportunities.

Personally, what I find most encouraging is younger students. Many of them don't see gender as a reason to hesitate before choosing a hard technical problem. They just go for it. To me, that shift in mindset is maybe the most important change, because it compounds. And I think those of us who are a bit further along have some responsibility to make that path easier, whether through mentoring, building inclusive teams, or simply making sure good work gets recognized no matter who did it.

r001.rationale: The response calls progress uneven, says some areas have stalled or reversed, and contrasts entry-level improvement with continued drop-offs at senior levels.

r002.rationale: The response describes changes in awareness and progress, but does not state that societal values concerning gender equality fluctuate.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, my answer is a bit of a mixed one.

If I look at the last ten years, there's clearly been progress on the surface. Conversations that used to feel awkward or taboo are now normal. Companies publish diversity numbers, conferences think about who's on the panel, and when I walk into a room of researchers today there are more women than when I started. Younger women I talk to seem to have fewer doubts about whether they belong in computer science at all, and that shift in default expectations matters a lot.

But I think the deeper layer has moved much more slowly. In my own field, systems and AI infrastructure, the ratio is still very lopsided, especially at the senior level and among the people who end up founding companies or leading the big technical efforts. The pipeline argument gets used a lot, but we've been fixing the pipeline for a decade and the top still looks pretty similar. That tells me the issue isn't only about getting people in the door. It's about who gets trusted with the important project, who gets the benefit of the doubt when something goes wrong, and who feels like they can push for an ambitious idea without being labeled difficult.

The other thing I'd say is that progress isn't evenly distributed. Tech in the Bay Area is one bubble. The experience of a woman engineer here is very different from a woman in a factory in another country, or even in a different industry in the same city. So when people say "society" has made progress, I always want to ask, which part of society.

I'd also be careful about assuming the direction is fixed. Some of the gains feel fragile. Economic downturns, layoffs, the shift to remote work and then back, all of those tend to hit women disproportionately, partly because of caregiving. And more recently there's been a bit of a backlash against anything with the word diversity attached to it, which makes some organizations quietly drop efforts they were only half committed to in the first place.

So my overall assessment: real progress in attitudes and visibility, modest progress in actual outcomes, and a lot of unfinished work on the structural side. I'm an optimist by nature, but I think the honest view is that the easy part is behind us and the hard part is ahead.

r001.rationale: The response describes uneven progress and says structural change has moved slowly, but it does not clearly state that any dimension has failed to improve.

r002.rationale: It says the direction is not fixed, describes a backlash against diversity, and notes that organizations are dropping efforts, communicating that views and commitments can shift.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ve made progress, but it’s uneven. Compared with ten years ago, people are more willing to talk about gender bias, workplace harassment, and the barriers women face in their careers. There’s also more awareness that equality involves how we hire, promote, pay, and share responsibilities at home.

But awareness doesn’t automatically translate into changes in everyday life. We still have to ask: Who gets opportunities? Whose judgment is trusted? Who takes on caregiving, and what does that mean for their career? Progress can look very different depending on someone’s circumstances.

So I’m cautiously optimistic. We have more language to describe the problems, and more willingness to challenge them. The next step is making sure that translates into lasting changes in institutions and everyday behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says progress is uneven and notes that increased awareness has not automatically changed everyday life, indicating that dimensions have not all improved equally.

r002.rationale: It describes greater willingness to discuss gender equality and uneven progress, but does not state that societal values fluctuate.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d say we’ve made progress, but it’s uneven. Compared with ten years ago, there’s more awareness of gender bias and more willingness to discuss issues like unequal pay, harassment, and barriers to leadership. That matters, because it’s difficult to change something people don’t acknowledge.

But awareness doesn’t automatically translate into equality. We still need to ask who gets hired, who gets promoted, whose ideas get heard, and who takes on caregiving responsibilities. People’s experiences also vary a great deal depending on where they live and their economic circumstances.

So I’m cautiously optimistic. The conversation has moved forward; the challenge now is making sure everyday practices and opportunities move forward with it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says progress is uneven and notes that greater awareness has not automatically translated into equality.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes greater awareness and discussion over time, but does not state that societal values fluctuate.
